narrative.text: A running header followed by the heading for the list of abbreviations.

Summarises the report, explaining that HSV2 is the main cause of genital ulcer disease, is very common where HIV epidemics are severe, and may facilitate HIV transmission in a two-way interaction. It notes that the workshop reviewed evidence and set priorities across epidemiology, HSV2–HIV interaction, therapy, vaccines and behavioural and microbicide studies.

Introduces the workshop by setting out the public health importance of HSV2 in developing countries and its suspected role in HIV spread. It explains that experts from developing and industrialized countries were invited to consider control measures.

States the workshop's objectives: to review knowledge on HSV2 epidemiology, its interaction with HIV, control measures and diagnostics, to identify knowledge gaps, and to set research and programme priorities.

Describes the 40 participants and the workshop's format of presentations, breakout groups and plenary prioritisation. It then reviews the epidemiology and natural history of HSV2, including rising prevalence worldwide and its role as the leading cause of genital ulcer disease. Table 1 gives seroprevalence figures for general populations in Africa, Latin America and Asia, and the section discusses HSV2 as a marker of sexual behaviour. It ends with recommended studies, including of discordant couples, with attention to counselling and treatment.

Explains the two-way biological interaction between HIV and HSV2, with HIV increasing HSV2 reactivation, shedding and severity, and HSV2 lesions containing HIV. It notes some evidence that aciclovir may prolong survival in people with HIV.

Continues the review of how HSV2 may increase HIV shedding, noting that aciclovir lowers both viruses in lesions and that data from developing countries are lacking. It lists recommended biological studies, such as whether the effect differs in Africa because of co-infections.

Summarises epidemiological evidence that HSV2 raises the risk of acquiring HIV, from a meta-analysis showing about a two-fold risk in men and weaker findings in women. It discusses why cross-sectional studies show stronger associations and recommends prospective studies and estimates of population attributable fractions.

Describes changes in the causes of genital ulcer disease in Africa, with Table 2 showing herpes rising and chancroid and syphilis falling at a South African mine clinic from 1986 to 1998. It notes that this undermines syndromic management and recommends monitoring ulcer causes by sex, HIV status and risk group.

Explains why clinical diagnosis of genital ulcers is unreliable where HIV is common and why rising herpes cases may increase syndromic treatment failure. It recommends lobbying for affordable aciclovir, evaluating its addition to syndromic algorithms, and strengthening health education.

Compares episodic and suppressive therapy for genital herpes with aciclovir, valaciclovir and famciclovir, summarising their effects on symptoms, shedding and recurrences. It considers how such therapy might reduce HIV transmission or acquisition. It recommends randomised trials in high-risk groups, such as serodiscordant couples and sex workers, with monitoring for drug resistance.

Discusses prophylactic and therapeutic HSV2 vaccines, the immune responses they should induce and the results of recent candidate vaccine trials. It considers how vaccine trials could be designed in developing countries, with HSV2 disease as the main endpoint and HIV infection as a secondary one.

Reviews other HSV2 prevention strategies where vaccines and therapy are not feasible, including behavioural interventions, condoms and female-controlled methods such as microbicides. It also covers counselling and states that widespread HSV2 screening was not recommended at that stage.

Describes how mathematical modelling has been used to understand HSV2 spread and its interaction with HIV, and summarises findings on antiviral treatment and behaviour change. It lists further modelling needs, such as drug resistance, cost-effectiveness and vaccine effects.

Reviews HSV2 diagnostic methods, including gold-standard Western blot, commercial ELISA tests, ways to measure incidence, and PCR detection of viral shedding. It lists research needs, such as evaluating assays on African sera and developing rapid tests for herpetic ulcers.

Introduces the agreed research and control priorities, starting with epidemiology and natural history, such as testing stored and sentinel surveillance sera for HSV2 prevalence and using cohort data to study the effect of HSV2 on HIV acquisition by sex and age.
Sets out the priority for clinical studies of how subclinical HSV2 shedding affects HIV shedding and transmission, ideally in areas with high rates of both infections.

Lists treatment-related priorities, including monitoring the causes of genital ulcers in clinic attenders by sex and HIV status, assessing aciclovir in syndromic management, and studying the effect of episodic therapy on HIV shedding. It also calls for randomised trials of suppressive therapy to prevent HIV in high-risk groups.
Proposes a working group to engage vaccine companies, lobby for prophylactic vaccine development and affordability in developing countries, and advance the DISC vaccine to later-phase trials.

Lists behavioural and microbicide priorities, including continued promotion of behaviour change and condoms, evaluation of HSV2 counselling and clinic management of herpes, and including HSV2 as an outcome in microbicide trials.
Recommends further modelling of HSV2 transmission and control, drug resistance, the cost-effectiveness of treatment strategies and the effects of vaccination on HIV.
Lists diagnostic priorities: rapid tests for herpes ulcers to guide syndromic management, and evaluation of serological tests on African sera.
Annex 1, the list of workshop participants with their institutions and contact details, running into the start of the reference list.
The reference list for the report, citing mainly studies on HSV2 epidemiology, treatment, vaccines and interaction with HIV, ending with WHO and UNAIDS contact details.

Front matter of the 2001 WHO/UNAIDS/LSHTM workshop report on herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV2) programmatic and research priorities in developing countries, with title pages, document numbers, ISBN and copyright notice, followed by a list of abbreviations. The extracted text also includes stray cover text from an unrelated WHO publication, Guidelines for the management of sexually transmitted infections.
